Main.sentence: The University of Washington ( UW [a] and informally U-Dub or U Dub[b] ) is a ___E:public U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university)___ ___E:research university U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university)___ in ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ , Washington, United States.
Founded in 1861, it is one of the oldest universities on the ___E:West Coast of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States)___ .

The university has a 700-acre (280 ha) ___E:main campus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campus_of_the_University_of_Washington)___ located in the city's ___E:University District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_District,_Seattle)___ .

It also has ___E:satellite campuses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_campus)___ in nearby cities of ___E:Tacoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Tacoma)___ and ___E:Bothell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Bothell)___ .

Overall, UW encompasses more than 500 buildings and over 20 million gross square footage of space, including one of the largest library systems in the world with more than 26 university libraries, art centers, museums, laboratories, lecture halls, and stadiums.

Washington is the ___E:flagship institution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship_university)___ of the ___E:six public universities in Washington State U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Washington_(state)#Public_institutions)___ .
It is known for its medical, engineering, and scientific research.
Washington is a member of the ___E:Association of American Universities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities)___ .

According to the ___E:National Science Foundation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation)___ , UW spent $1.73 billion on research and development in 2024, ranking it fifth in the nation.

Its 22 varsity sports teams compete as the ___E:Huskies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies)___ in the ___E:Big Ten Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference)___ of ___E:NCAA Division I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I)___ , and represent the United States at the ___E:Olympic Games U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games)___ and other competitions.

In 1854, territorial governor ___E:Isaac Stevens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Stevens)___ recommended the establishment of a university in the ___E:Washington Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Territory)___ .

Prominent Seattle-area residents, including ___E:Methodist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist)___ preacher ___E:Daniel Bagley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Bagley)___ , saw this as a chance to add to the city's potential and prestige.
Bagley learned of a law that allowed United States territories to sell land to raise money in support of public schools.

At the time, ___E:Arthur A. Denny U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_A._Denny)___ , one of the founders of Seattle and a member of the territorial legislature, aimed to increase the city's importance by moving the territory's capital from ___E:Olympia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia,_Washington)___ to Seattle.
However, Bagley ultimately persuaded Denny that founding a university would better contribute to the growth of Seattle's economy.

Two universities were initially chartered, but later the decision was repealed in favor of a single university in ___E:Lewis County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_County,_Washington)___ provided that locally donated land was available.
When no site emerged, Denny successfully petitioned the legislature to reconsider Seattle as a location in 1858.
In 1861, scouting began for an appropriate 10 acres (4 ha) site in Seattle to serve as a new university campus.

Arthur and Mary Denny donated eight acres, while fellow pioneers Edward Lander, and Charlie and Mary Terry, donated two acres on Denny's Knoll in ___E:downtown Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown,_Seattle,_Washington)___ .
More specifically, this tract was bounded by 4th Avenue to the west, 6th Avenue to the east, Union Street to the north, and Seneca Streets to the south.
John Pike, for whom ___E:Pike Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_Street_(Seattle))___ is named, was the university's architect and builder.
It was opened on November 4, 1861, as the Territorial University of Washington.

The legislature passed articles incorporating the university, and establishing its Board of Regents in 1862. The school initially struggled, closing three times: in 1863 for low enrollment, and again in 1867 and 1876 for shortage of funds.
Washington awarded its first graduate ___E:Clara Antoinette McCarty Wilt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Antoinette_McCarty_Wilt)___ in 1876, with a Bachelor of Science degree.

By the time ___E:Washington state U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state))___ entered the ___E:Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ in 1889, both Seattle and the university had grown substantially.
Washington's total undergraduate enrollment increased from 30 to nearly 300 students, and the campus's relative isolation in downtown Seattle faced encroaching development.

A special legislative committee, headed by UW graduate ___E:Edmond Meany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Meany)___ , was created to find a new campus to better serve the growing student population and faculty.

The committee eventually selected a site on the northeast of ___E:downtown Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown,_Seattle,_Washington)___ called ___E:Union Bay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Bay_(Seattle,_Washington))___ , which was the land of the ___E:Duwamish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duwamish_people)___ , and the legislature appropriated funds for its purchase and construction.
In 1895, the university relocated to the new campus by moving into the newly built ___E:Denny Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_Hall)___ .

The University Regents tried and failed to sell the old campus, eventually settling with leasing the area. This later became one of the university's most valuable pieces of real estate in modern-day Seattle, generating millions in annual revenue with what is now called the ___E:Metropolitan Tract U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Tract_(Seattle))___ .
The original Territorial University building was torn down in 1908, and its former site now houses the ___E:Fairmont Olympic Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmont_Olympic_Hotel)___ .
The sole-surviving remnants of Washington's first building are four 24-foot (7.3 m), white, hand-fluted cedar, Ionic columns.
They were salvaged by ___E:Edmond S. Meany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_S._Meany)___ , one of the university's first graduates and former head of its history department.

Meany and his colleague, Dean Herbert T. Condon, dubbed the columns as "Loyalty," "Industry," "Faith", and "Efficiency", or "LIFE." The columns now stand in the ___E:Sylvan Grove Theater U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvan_Grove_Theater_and_Columns)___ .

Organizers of the 1909 ___E:Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska%E2%80%93Yukon%E2%80%93Pacific_Exposition)___ eyed the still largely undeveloped campus as a prime setting for their ___E:world's fair U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Fair)___ .

They came to an agreement with Washington's ___E:Board of Regents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Regents)___ that allowed them to use the campus grounds for the exposition, surrounding today's ___E:Drumheller Fountain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drumheller_Fountain)___ facing towards ___E:Mount Rainier U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier)___ .
In exchange, organizers agreed Washington would take over the campus and its development after the fair's conclusion.
This arrangement led to a detailed site plan and several new buildings, prepared in part by ___E:John Charles Olmsted U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Charles_Olmsted)___ .
The plan was later incorporated into the overall UW campus master plan, permanently affecting the campus layout.
Both ___E:World Wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War)___ brought the military to campus, with certain facilities temporarily lent to the federal government.
In spite of this, subsequent post-war periods were times of dramatic growth for the university.
The ___E:period between the wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interwar_period)___ saw a significant expansion of the upper campus.

Construction of the ___E:Liberal Arts Quadrangle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Arts_Quadrangle)___ , known to students as "The Quad," began in 1916 and continued to 1939. The university's architectural centerpiece, ___E:Suzzallo Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzzallo_Library)___ , was built in 1926 and expanded in 1935.

In 1942, all ___E:persons of Japanese ancestry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Americans)___ in the Seattle area were forced into inland ___E:internment camps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment_of_Japanese_Americans)___ as part of ___E:Executive Order 9066 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_9066)___ following the attack on ___E:Pearl Harbor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Harbor)___ .

During this difficult time, university president ___E:Lee Paul Sieg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Paul_Sieg)___ took an active and sympathetic leadership role in advocating for and facilitating the transfer of Japanese American students to universities and colleges away from the Pacific Coast to help them avoid the mass incarceration.
Nevertheless, many Japanese American students and "soon-to-be" graduates were unable to transfer successfully in the short time window or receive diplomas before being incarcerated.

It was only many years later that they were recognized for their accomplishments, during the University of Washington's ___E:Long Journey Home U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Long_Journey_Home_(ceremonial_event))___ ceremonial event that was held in May 2008.

On October 2, 1946, the University of Washington formally opened a medical school as part of a School of Health Sciences against the Washington State Medical Association's oppositions, who did not wish to create a competitive surplus of physicians.

The operation was spearheaded by President ___E:Henry Suzzallo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Suzzallo)___ based on plans created by ___E:Gideon Weed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gideon_A._Weed)___ , ___E:Rufus Willard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rufus_Willard&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , and ___E:Thomas Minor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Minor)___ earlier in 1884. The ___E:G.I. Bill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Bill_of_Rights)___ was later created and passed, establishing the School of Health Sciences while providing $3.75 million for buildings and $450,000 for salaries.
This was the foundation for the ___E:University of Washington Medical Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Medical_Center)___ , ranked by U.S.
News & World Report as one of the top ten hospitals in the nation.

The School of Health Sciences was later renamed the ___E:School of Medicine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_School_of_Medicine)___ in 1946, which is now consistently ranked as the top medical school in the United States.

The University of Washington's role as a medical school sharply drew more attention after the ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ boom in wartime industry and economics.

___E:J. Robert Oppenheimer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Robert_Oppenheimer)___ was nominated in 1954 by the University of Washington's Physics Department to lecture physics students for one week, but was unable to attend because of loyalty checks asked for by the ___E:US Federal Government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Federal_Government)___ .
Oppenheimer never accepted the invitations, and ___E:President Dr. Henry Schmitz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Schmitz)___ disapproved of his nomination.

From 1958 to 1973, the University of Washington saw a tremendous growth in student enrollment, its faculties and operating budget, and also its prestige under the leadership of ___E:Charles Odegaard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Odegaard)___ .

During this period, the faculty was sharply divided over the issues of the role of the faculty in faculty appointments, and the conflict of who should run the University, the faculty or the parents and taxpayers.

Henry Schmitz characterized the matter as "an internal power struggle."  UW student enrollment had more than doubled to 34,000 as the ___E:baby boom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-World_War_II_baby_boom)___ generation came of age.

The University of Washington has a long history with civil rights starting from 1874,  through 1899  with civil activism and through 1968     to 1975. This era was also marked by high levels of ___E:student activism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_activism)___ , as was the case at many American universities.

Much of the unrest focused around ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ , actively seen when football coach Jim Owens suspended four Black football players on October 30, 1969, for "[a] lack of commitment to the team," after which activists demanded Owen's resignation and the rest of the black football players on the team refused to play.  For a time, activists had been passionate as to incite a response from school administration to occupy the campus after the activists harmed 17 persons.

African American Dr. Robert Flennaugh was appointed to the UW Board of Regents on March 25, 1970  and later on June 22 the University of Washington Daily eliminated gender-based help ads.  Activism peaked in 1975 when 2,000 students protested university hiring practices on the campus through May 13 and 14.  Further opposition to the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ occurred,  and in response to anti-Vietnam War protests by the late 1960s, the University Safety and Security Division became the University of Washington Police Department.
On June 29, 1969, a bomb detonated on campus, causing $100,000 in damages and no injuries.
No group claimed responsibility for the incident.
Odegaard instituted a vision of building a "community of scholars", convincing the Washington State legislatures to increase investment in the university.

Washington ___E:senators U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate)___ , such as ___E:Henry M. Jackson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_M._Jackson)___ and ___E:Warren G. Magnuson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Magnuson)___ , also used their political clout to gather research funds for UW. The results included an increase in the operating budget from $37 million in 1958 to over $400 million in 1973, solidifying UW as a top recipient of federal research funds in the United States.

The establishment of technology giants such as ___E:Microsoft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)___ , ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ and ___E:Amazon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com)___ in the local area also proved to be highly influential in the UW's fortunes, not only improving graduate prospects   but also helping to attract millions of dollars in university and research funding through its distinguished faculty and extensive alumni network.

In 1990, the University of Washington opened its additional campuses in ___E:Bothell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Bothell)___ and ___E:Tacoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Tacoma)___ .
Originally designed for students who had completed two years of higher education, both schools have since evolved into four-year universities with the authority to award degrees.
The first freshman classes were admitted in the fall of 2006. Today, both the Bothell and Tacoma campuses also offer a range of master's degree programs.

In 2012, the university began exploring plans and governmental approval to expand the main ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ campus, including significant increases in student housing, teaching facilities for the growing student body and faculty, as well as expanded public transit options.

The ___E:University of Washington light rail station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_light_rail_station)___ was completed in March 2016,  connecting Seattle's ___E:Capitol Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Hill_(Seattle))___ neighborhood to the UW Husky Stadium within five minutes of rail travel time.  It offers a previously unavailable option of transportation into and out of the campus, designed specifically to reduce dependence on private vehicles, bicycles and local ___E:King County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_County,_Washington)___ buses.

On January 23, 1939, the University of Washington was criticized for hiring Economics Professor ___E:Harold J. Laski U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Laski)___ , a British ___E:Marxist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxian_economics)___ , as a visiting lecturer  in between the ___E:First Red Scare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Red_Scare)___ and ___E:Second Red Scare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism)___ .

The University of Washington was highly suspect by the ___E:Truman Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Harry_S._Truman)___ in 1948 and 1949. ___E:Thomas H. Bienz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Thomas_Bienz&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , a ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:State senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_senator)___ , declared that "At least 150 [University faculty members] are ___E:Communists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism)___ " and soon thereafter two investigations were started by the ___E:Canwell Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canwell_Committee)___ and the University.

Professor of philosophy Herbert Phillips, professor of ___E:old English literature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_literature)___ Joe Butterworth and professor of ___E:social psychology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_psychology)___ Ralph Gundlach were dismissed after the investigations.

A year after, another second investigation was commenced by the ___E:Joint Legislative Fact-finding Committee on Un-American Activities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canwell_Committee)___ in the State of Washington, leading to investigations into other professors with a response of "One hundred and three professors [signing] an open letter to the University of Washington Board of Regents that stated the firings were based on guilt by association.
The letter also declared that faculty morale and the University's reputation was damaged."

The original proposal of the University included increases for research scientists of about 10% over three years plus changes in the pay structure and a catch-up increase of 3.25% for those who did not get a merit raise last year. For postdocs, the original UW offer was an average 15% total wage increase in 2023, including 13% in January when new minimums were introduced, plus higher minimum salaries.

UW's main campus is situated in ___E:Seattle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)___ , by the shores of ___E:Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Bay_(Seattle,_Washington))___ and ___E:Portage Bays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portage_Bay)___ with views of the ___E:Cascade Range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Range)___ to the east, and the ___E:Olympic Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Mountains)___ to the west. The site encompasses 700 acres (2.8 km 2 ) bounded by N.E. 45th Street on the north, N.E.
Pacific Street on the south, Montlake Boulevard N.E. on the east, and 15th Avenue N.E. on the west.

___E:Red Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Square_(University_of_Washington))___ is the heart of the campus, surrounded by landmark buildings and artworks, such as ___E:Suzzallo Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzzallo_Library)___ , the Broken Obelisk , and the ___E:statue of George Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_George_Washington_(Seattle))___ .
It functions as the central hub for students and hosts a variety of events annually.
University Way, known locally as " ___E:The Ave U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ave)___ ", lies nearby and is a focus for much student life at the university.

North Campus features some of UW's most recognized landscapes as well as landmarks, stretching from the signature ___E:University of Washington Quad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Quad)___ directly north of ___E:Red Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Square_(University_of_Washington))___ to N.E. 45th Street,  and encompasses a number of the university's most historical academic, research, housing, parking, recreational and administrative buildings.

With UW's continued growth, administrators proposed a new, multimillion-dollar, multi-phase development plan in late 2014 to refine portions of the North Campus, renovating and replacing old student housing with new ___E:LEED-certified U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design)___ complexes, introducing new academic facilities, sports fields, open greenery, and museums.

The UW ___E:Foster School of Business U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foster_School_of_Business)___ , ___E:School of Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_School_of_Law)___ , and the ___E:Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Culture)___ , which houses a significant number of exhibits including a 66-million-year-old ___E:Tyrannosaurus rex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus)___ fossil skull – one of only 15 known to exist in the world today and part of an ongoing excavation, are also located in North Campus.
The ___E:U District light rail station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U_District_station)___ is just west of the Burke Museum.
South Campus occupies the land between Pacific Street and the ___E:Lake Washington Ship Canal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Washington_Ship_Canal)___ .

The land was previously the site of the University Golf Course but was given up to construct a building for the ___E:School of Medicine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_School_of_Medicine)___ .

Today, South Campus is the location of UW's health sciences and natural sciences facilities, including the ___E:UW Medical Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Medical_Center)___ and the ___E:Magnuson Health Sciences Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Magnuson_Health_Sciences_Center)___ as well as locations for instruction and research in oceanography, ___E:bioengineering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_Department_of_Bioengineering)___ , biology, genome sciences, hydraulics, and comparative medicine.

The East Campus area stretches east of Montlake Boulevard to ___E:Laurelhurst U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurelhurst,_Seattle,_Washington)___ and is largely taken up by ___E:wetlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetland)___  and Huskies sports facilities and recreation fields, including ___E:Husky Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky_Stadium)___ , ___E:Hec Edmundson Pavilion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hec_Edmundson_Pavilion)___ , and ___E:Husky Ballpark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky_Ballpark)___ .

The area directly north of the sports facilities is home to UW's computer science and engineering programs, which includes ___E:computer labs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_lab)___ once used by ___E:Paul G. Allen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Allen)___ and ___E:Bill Gates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates)___ for their ___E:prior venture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traf-O-Data)___ before establishing Microsoft.

In 2019, the ___E:Bill & Melinda Gates Center For Computer Science & Engineering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_G._Allen_School_of_Computer_Science_%26_Engineering#Buildings)___ opened in East Campus.
Located adjacent is the Mechanical Engineering Building, home to the Industrial and Systems Engineering program.

The area northeast of the sports facilities is occupied by components of the UW Botanic Gardens, such as the ___E:Union Bay Natural Area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Bay_Natural_Area)___ , the UW Farm, and the Center for Urban Horticulture.

Further east is the ___E:Ceramic and Metal Arts Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceramic_and_Metal_Arts_Building)___ and Laurel Village, which provides family housing for registered full-time students.
East Campus is also the location of the ___E:UW light rail station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UW_light_rail_station)___ .

West Campus consists of mainly ___E:modernist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_architecture)___ structures located on city streets, and stretches between 15th Avenue and ___E:Interstate 5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_5)___ from the Ship Canal, to N.E. 41st Street.

It is home to the College of Built Environments, School of Social Work, Fishery Sciences Building, UW Police Department as well as many of the university's apartments such as Stevens Court and Mercer Court and residence halls Alder, Lander, Maple and Elm Hall.

The University of Washington Board of Regents governs the University of Washington per the ___E:Revised Code of Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Code_of_Washington)___ 28B.20.130 statute.
The board is responsible for selecting, overseeing, and assessing the ___E:university president U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_University_of_Washington)___ .
Generally, the Board of Regents entrusts the president with the daily operations of the university, in collaboration with the faculty and in line with legal provisions.
The Board of Regents is made up of eleven members, including one student member and one faculty member.

Regents are appointed by the ___E:governor of the State of Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Washington)___ for six-year terms, except for the Student Regent (who serves for one year) and the Faculty Regent (who serves for three years).
Regents continue to serve after their terms have ended until either they resign or the governor appoints a successor.
Officers of the board are elected annually at the September meeting.

One of the most notable former regents is ___E:William Henry Gates II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates_Sr.)___ , the father of ___E:Bill Gates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates)___ .
William Henry Gates II served as a regent from 1997 to 2012.

___E:Environmental sustainability U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_sustainability)___ has long been a major focus of the university's Board of Regents and Presidents.

In February 2006, UW joined a partnership with ___E:Seattle City Light U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_City_Light)___ as part of their Green Up Program, ensuring that all of Seattle campus' electricity is supplied by and purchased from renewable sources.

In 2010, then UW President Emmert furthered the university's efforts with a host of other universities across the U.S., and signed the ___E:American College & University Presidents' Climate Commitment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_College_%26_University_Presidents%27_Climate_Commitment)___ .
UW created a Climate Action Team,  as well as an Environmental Stewardship Advisory Committee (ESAC) which keeps track of UW's greenhouse gas emissions and carbon footprint.
Policies were enacted with environmental stewardship in mind, and institutional support was provided to assist with campus sustainability.
Overall, the University of Washington was one of several universities to receive the highest grade, "A−", on the Sustainable Endowments Institute's College Sustainability Report Card in 2011.
The University of Washington is an active member of the ___E:University of the Arctic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Arctic)___ .

UArctic is an international cooperative network based in the Circumpolar Arctic region, consisting of more than 200 universities, colleges, and other organizations with an interest in promoting education and research in the Arctic region.
The university also participates in UArctic's mobility program north2north.
The aim of that program is to enable students of member institutions to study in different parts of the North.

The university offers bachelor's, master's and ___E:doctoral U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctoral_degree)___ degrees through its 140 departments, themselves organized into various colleges and schools.

It also continues to operate a ___E:Transition School and Early Entrance Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_School_and_Early_Entrance_Program)___ on campus, which first began in 1977.

UW is an elected member of the ___E:American Association of Universities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_of_Universities)___ , and has been listed as a " ___E:Public Ivy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Ivy)___ " in ___E:Greene's Guides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Ivy#Greenes'_Guides_list_(2001))___ since 2001.
The Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) has consistently ranked UW as one of the top 20 universities worldwide every year since its first release.

In 2019, UW ranked 14th worldwide out of 500 by the ARWU , 26th worldwide out of 981 in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings , and 28th worldwide out of 101 in the Times ___E:World Reputation Rankings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Reputation_Rankings)___ .
Meanwhile, QS World University Rankings ranked it 68th worldwide, out of over 900.
U.S.

News & World Report ranked UW 6th out of nearly 1,500 universities worldwide for 2024, with UW's undergraduate program tied for 40th among 389 national universities in the U.S. and tied for 19th among 209 public universities.
In 2019, it ranked 10th among the universities around the world by ___E:SCImago Institutions Rankings U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCImago_Institutions_Rankings)___ .
In 2019, Kiplinger magazine's review of "top college values" named UW 5th for in-state students and 10th for out-of-state students among U.S. public colleges, and 84th overall out of 500 schools.

In the Washington Monthly National University Rankings UW was ranked 15th domestically in 2018, based on its contribution to the public good as measured by social mobility, research, and promoting public service.

In 2017, the ___E:Leiden Ranking U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CWTS_Leiden_Ranking)___ , which focuses on science and the impact of scientific publications among the world's 500 major universities, ranked UW 12th globally and 5th in the U.S.

The university does not require submission of either ___E:SAT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT)___ or ___E:ACT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(test))___ scores for admission, and the university position is that those scores are "not considered for admission, even if submitted (test blind)".

In 2024, newly enrolled students had a median high school ___E:GPA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_grading_in_the_United_States#Grade_conversion)___ of 3.82.  The university's undergraduate admissions process is rated 91/99 by the ___E:Princeton Review U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_Review)___ ,   and is classified "more selective" by the U.S.
News & World Report .
For the Class of 2025 (enrolled fall 2021), UW received 48,840 applications and accepted 26,121 (53.5%).

Of those accepted, 7,252 enrolled, a ___E:yield rate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yield_(college_admissions))___ (the percentage of accepted students who choose to attend the university) of 27.8%.
UW's freshman ___E:retention rate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_student_retention)___ is 93%, with 84% going on to graduate within six years.

Of the 19% of the incoming freshman class who submitted ___E:SAT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT)___ scores; the middle 50 percent Composite scores were 1240–1450.  Of the 8% of enrolled freshmen in 2021 who submitted ___E:ACT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(test))___ scores; the middle 50 percent Composite score was between 29 and 34.  In the 2020–2021 academic year, 24 freshman students were ___E:National Merit Scholars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Merit_Scholars)___ .
The university uses capacity constrained majors,  a gate-keeping process that requires most students to apply to an internal college or faculty.

New applications are usually considered once or twice annually, and few students are admitted each time.  The screening process is based on cumulative academic performance, recommendation letters and extracurricular activities.
UW's research budget surpassed the $1.0 billion research budget milestone in 2012,  and university endowments reached almost $5.0 billion by 2021.

In 2014, the University of Washington School of Oceanography and the UW Applied Physics Laboratory completed the construction of the first ___E:high-power underwater cabled observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Scale_Nodes)___ in the United States. ___E:Gabrielle Rocap U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabrielle_Rocap)___ , one of the researchers who discovered arsenic-breathing microbes in the Pacific, is part of the department's faculty.

To promote equal academic opportunity, especially for people of low income, UW launched Husky Promise in 2006. Families of income up to 65 percent of state median income or 235 percent of the federal poverty level are eligible.
With this, up to 30 percent of undergraduate students may be eligible.
The cut-off income level that UW set is the highest in the nation, making top-quality education available to more people.
UW President Mark Emmert said that being "elitist is not in our DNA".

UW was the host university of ___E:ResearchChannel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ResearchChannel)___ program (now defunct), the only TV channel in the United States dedicated solely for the dissemination of research from academic institutions and research organizations.
Participation of ResearchChannel included 36 universities, 15 research organizations, two corporate research centers and many other affiliates.

Alan Michelson, now Head of the Built Environments Library at UW Seattle, manages the Pacific Coast Architecture Database (PCAD), which Michelson started in 2002 while he worked as Architecture and Design Librarian at the ___E:University of California, Los Angeles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles)___ (UCLA).

The PCAD serves as a searchable public database detailing significant but importantly, also lesser-known and -lauded designers, buildings and structures, and partnerships, with links including to bibliographic literature.

In 2019, iDefense reported that ___E:Chinese hackers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberwarfare_and_China)___ had launched ___E:cyberattacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_espionage_in_the_United_States)___ on dozens of academic institutions in an attempt to gain information on technology being developed for the ___E:United States Navy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy)___ .
Some of the targets included the University of Washington.
The attacks have been underway since at least April 2017.

The University of Washington had 50,097 total enrollments as of fall 2023, making it the largest university on the ___E:West Coast U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States)___ by student population in spite of its selective admissions process.

It also boasts one of the most diverse student bodies within the US, with more than 50% of its undergraduate students self-identifying with ___E:minority groups U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_group)___ .
The University of Washington boasts over 800 active Registered Student Organizations (RSOs), one of the largest networks of any universities in the world.
RSOs are dedicated to a wide variety of interests both in and beyond campus.

Some of these interest areas include academic focus groups, cultural exchanges, environmental activities, Greek life, political/social action, religious discussions, sports, international student gatherings by country, and STEM-specific events.
The Associated Students of the University of Washington (ASUW) is one of two student governments at the University of Washington, the other being the Graduate and Professional Student Senate.

It is funded and supported by student fees, and provides services that directly and indirectly benefit them. The ASUW employs over 72 current University of Washington students, has over 500 volunteers, and spends $1.03 million annually to provide services and activities to the student body of 43,000 on-campus.
The Student Senate was established in 1994 as a division of the Associated Students of the University of Washington.
Student Senate is one of two official student-governed bodies and provides a broad-based discussion of issues.
Currently, the ASUW Student Senate has a legislative body of over 150 senators representing a diverse set of interests on and off-campus.

The ASUW was incorporated in the State of Washington in 1906.  The ___E:ASUW Experimental College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASUW_Experimental_College)___ , part of the ASUW, was created in 1968 by several University of Washington students seeking to provide the campus and surrounding community with a selection of non-credit classes not offered on the university curriculum.
The Experimental College ceased operation in 2017.
The student newspaper is The Daily of the University of Washington .
It is the second-largest [clarification needed] daily paper in Seattle.

In 2010, The Daily launched a half-hour weekly television magazine show, The Daily's Double Shot , on ___E:UWTV U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UWTV)___ Channel 27. UW continues to use its proprietary UWTV channel, online and printed publications.
The faculty also produce their own publications for students and alumni.
The Tyee was the official student ___E:yearbook U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook)___ of the University of Washington.

Throughout the 20th century, UW student activism centered around a variety of national and international concerns, from ___E:nuclear energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power)___ to the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ and ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ .

In 1948, at the beginning of the ___E:McCarthyism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism)___ era, students brought their activism to bear on campus by protesting the firing of three UW professors accused of communist affiliations.
In May 2025, pro-Palestinian protestors caused approximately $1 million in damage to the school's Interdisciplinary Engineering Building. 31 people were arrested.
The university operates one of the largest campuses of any higher education institution in the world.
Despite this, growing faculty and student count has strained the regional housing supply as well as transportation facilities.
Starting in 2012, UW began taking active measures to explore, plan and enact a series of campus policies to manage the annual growth.

In addition to new buildings, parking and ___E:light rail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail)___ stations, new building construction and renovations have been scheduled to take place through 2020.  The plan includes the construction of three six-story ___E:residence halls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residence_hall)___ and two apartment complexes in the west section of campus, near the existing ___E:Terry and Lander Halls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_and_Lander_Halls)___ , in Phase I, the renovation of six existing residence halls in Phase II, and additional new construction in Phase III. The projects will result in a net gain of approximately 2,400 beds. The Residence Hall Student Association (student government for the halls) is the second-largest student organization on campus and helps plan fun events in the halls.
For students, faculty, and staff looking to live off-campus, they may also explore Off-Campus Housing Affairs.
The Greek system at UW has also been a prominent part of student culture for more than 115 years.
It is made up of two organizational bodies, the ___E:Interfraternity Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interfraternity_Council)___ (IFC) and the Panhellenic Association.
The IFC looks over 34 fraternities with 1,900+ members, and Panhellenic consists of 19 sororities and 1,900 members.
The school has additional Greek organizations that do not offer housing and are primarily special-interest.

In addition to the University of Washington's Disability Resources for Students (DRS) office, there is also a campus-wide ___E:DO-IT (Disabilities, Opportunities, Internetworking, and Technology) Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_DO-IT_Center)___ program that assists educational institutions to fully integrate all students, including those with disabilities, into academic life. DO-IT includes a variety of initiatives, such as the ___E:DO-IT Scholars Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DO-IT_Scholars_Program)___ , and provides information on the "universal" design of educational facilities for students of all levels of physical and mental ability.
These design programs aim to reduce systemic barriers which could otherwise hinder the performance of some students, and may also be applied to other professional organizations and conferences.
UW students, sports teams, and alumni are called ___E:Washington Huskies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies)___ .

The ___E:husky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky)___ was selected as the school mascot by the student committee in 1922, which replaced the "Sun Dodger", an abstract reference to the ___E:local weather U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle,_Washington#Climate)___ .

The university participates in the ___E:National Collegiate Athletic Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association)___ 's ___E:Division I FBS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Football_Bowl_Subdivision)___ .

It is a member of the ___E:Big Ten Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference)___ , after having been in the ___E:Pac-12 Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-12_Conference)___ for decades prior until the ___E:2024 conference realignment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932024_NCAA_conference_realignment)___ .

The ___E:football team U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies_football)___ is traditionally competitive, having won the 1960 and 1991 national title and appeared in the ___E:College Football Playoff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_Playoff)___ in 2016 and 2023, to go along with seven ___E:Rose Bowl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Bowl_Game)___ victories and single wins in the ___E:Orange Bowl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Bowl)___ and ___E:Sugar Bowl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Bowl)___ .

From 1907 to 1917, Washington football teams were unbeaten in 64 consecutive games, an ___E:NCAA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association)___ record.  ___E:Tailgating U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailgate_party)___ by boat has been a Husky Stadium tradition since 1920 when the stadium was first built on the shores of ___E:Lake Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Washington)___ .

The ___E:Apple Cup U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Cup)___ game is an annual game against cross-state rival ___E:Washington State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Cougars_football)___ that was first contested in 1900 with UW leading the all-time series, 75 wins to 33 losses and 6 ties. Following the 2024 conference realignment—which resulted with UW and WSU in separate conferences—the schools agreed to continue the Apple Cup "through at least 2028."  This game was last won by the University of Washington, and the Apple Cup trophy currently resides in Seattle. ___E:College Football Hall of Fame U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_Hall_of_Fame)___ member ___E:Don James U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_James_(American_football))___ is a former head coach.

The men's ___E:basketball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies_men%27s_basketball)___ team has been moderately successful, though recently the team has enjoyed a resurgence under coach ___E:Lorenzo Romar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Romar)___ .

With Romar as head coach, the team has been to six ___E:NCAA tournaments U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men%27s_Division_I_Basketball_Championship)___ (2003–2004, 2004–2005, 2005–2006, 2008–2009, 2009–2010 and 2010–2011 seasons), 2 consecutive top 16 (sweet sixteen) appearances, and secured a No. 1 seed in 2005. On December 23, 2005, the men's basketball team won their 800th victory in Hec Edmundson Pavilion, the most wins for any NCAA team in its current arena.

___E:Rowing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_rowing_(United_States))___ is a longstanding tradition at the University of Washington dating back to 1901. The Washington men's crew gained international prominence by winning the ___E:gold medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal)___ at the ___E:1936 Summer Olympics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics)___ in Berlin, defeating the German and Italian crews much to the dismay of ___E:Adolf Hitler U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler)___ who was in attendance.
The team was depicted in the 2013 bestseller The Boys in the Boat .

In 1958, the men's crew deepened their legend with a shocking win over ___E:Leningrad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg)___ Trud's world champion rowers at the Moscow Cup, resulting in the first American sporting victory on Soviet soil,   and certainly the first time a Russian crowd gave any American team a standing ovation during the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ .

The men's crew have won 46 national titles  (15 ___E:Intercollegiate Rowing Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercollegiate_Rowing_Association)___ , 1 ___E:National Collegiate Rowing Championship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Rowing_Championship)___ ), 15 Olympic gold medals, two silver and five bronze.
The women have 10 national titles and two Olympic gold medals.
In 1997, the women's team won the NCAA championship.
The Husky men are the 2015 national champions.

Recent national champions include the ___E:softball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies_softball)___ team ( ___E:2009 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Women%27s_College_World_Series)___ ), the men's rowing team (2015, 2014, 2013, 2012, 2011, 2009, 2007), NCAA Division I women's ___E:cross country U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running)___ team (2008), and the women's volleyball team ( ___E:2005 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NCAA_Division_I_women%27s_volleyball_tournament)___ ).

Individually, Scott Roth was the 2011 NCAA men's Outdoor ___E:Pole Vault U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pole_Vault)___ and 2011 & 2010 NCAA men's Indoor Pole Vault champion. ___E:James Lepp U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lepp)___ was the 2005 NCAA men's golf champion.

Ryan Brown (men's 800 meters) and Amy Lia (women's 1500 meters) won individual titles at the 2006 NCAA Track and Field Championships. ___E:Brad Walker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Walker_(athlete))___ was the 2005 NCAA men's Outdoor and Indoor Pole Vault champion.

The university has an extensive series of sports facilities, including but not limited to the ___E:Husky Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky_Stadium)___ (football, track and field), the ___E:Alaska Airlines Arena at Hec Edmundson Pavilion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hec_Edmundson_Pavilion)___ (basketball, volleyball, and gymnastics), ___E:Husky Ballpark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky_Ballpark)___ (baseball), Husky Softball Stadium, The ___E:Bill Quillian Tennis Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Quillian_(athlete))___ , The ___E:Nordstrom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordstrom)___ Tennis Center, Dempsey Indoor (Indoor track and field, football) and the ___E:Conibear Shellhouse U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conibear_Shellhouse)___ (rowing).

The golf team plays at the Washington National Golf Club and until recently, the swimming team called the ___E:Weyerhaeuser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyerhaeuser)___ Aquatic Center and the Husky pool home. The university discontinued its men's and women's swim teams on May 1, 2009, due to budget cuts.
The rebuilt Husky Stadium is the first and primary source of income for the completely remodeled athletic district.

The major remodel consisted of a new grand concourse, ___E:underground light-rail station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington_station)___ which opened on March 19, 2016,  an enclosed west end design, replacement of bleachers with individual seating, removal of track and Huskytron, as well as the installation of a new press box section, private box seating, football offices, permanent seating in the east end zone that does not block the view of Lake Washington.
The project also included new and improved amenities, concession stands, and bathrooms throughout.

The cost for renovating the stadium was around $280 million and was designed for a slightly lower ___E:seating capacity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seating_capacity)___ than its previous design, now at 70,138 seats.
The university calls the stadium the "Greatest Setting in College Football."

The University of Washington's costumed mascot is ___E:Harry the Husky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_the_Husky)___ . "Harry the Husky" performs at sporting and special events, and a live ___E:Alaskan Malamute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaskan_Malamute)___ , currently named Dubs II,  has traditionally led the UW ___E:football U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football)___ team onto the field at the start of games.

The school colors of purple and gold were adopted in 1892 by student vote. The choice was inspired by the first ___E:stanza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanza)___ of ___E:Lord Byron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Byron)___ 's The Destruction of Sennacherib :

The ___E:Assyrian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyria)___ came down like the wolf on the fold, And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold; And the sheen of their spears was like stars on the sea, When the blue wave rolls nightly on deep ___E:Galilee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Galilee)___ .
The university has also hosted a long line of Alaskan Malamutes as mascots.

The first UW power plant was built simultaneously with some of the first campus buildings back in 1895, and was located to the east of campus along the existing shoreline of ___E:Lake Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Washington)___ .
The plant, which burned coal to produce steam to help heat and electrify the campus, was quickly replaced in 1901 as the campus’ energy needs began to grow.
This second power plant was located where the modern day Allen Library stands.
It too used a coal and steam system, and was in use for 7 years before it was put to rest and a third plant was built.
This third power plant, which originally consisted of two 250 horsepower coal powered boilers, remains the current site for the University of Washington's central power plant.
It is located opposite Montlake Boulevard from the Intramural Activities Building (IMA).
The university started their switch from coal to natural gas in 1956 and finished in 1988, motivated by growing global environmental concerns and awareness.

An additional power plant, the West Campus Utility Plant (WCUP), was added to campus in 2017.  This plant serves as a backup power supply to research buildings on Southwest campus, and generates and stores chilled water for cooling purposes.
The current capacity of this plant is 6 megawatts of emergency power and 4,500 tons of chilled water, but is expandable to double the size of both reserves with no necessary building modifications.

The WCUP was awarded the Envision Gold Award from the ___E:Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Sustainable_Infrastructure)___ for its sustainability focused building design and purposes.
___E:Fossil fuels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_fuel)___ are still tightly embedded in energy systems across the world.

This is reflected in the university's energy production, as they still rely on ___E:natural gas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas)___ to heat most of its buildings, despite their clean energy goals and commitments.
It was found that as of 2024, 93% of the university's direct greenhouse gas emissions originated from the natural gas combustion system within the UW's central power plant.

The heat produced using natural gas is transported through 8 miles of underground utility tunnels that connect to campus buildings, alongside side electrical lines, communication lines, and internet cables.

Although electric chillers are already in place, which cool water down as a form of AC to then be pumped into buildings through the utility tunnels,  the university hopes to switch the heating processes from natural gas to electric heat pumps in order to meet their clean energy goals.

In contrast from the current heating systems, most of the UW's electric power is supplied by ___E:Seattle City Light U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_City_Light)___ , who generates the majority of their electricity through ___E:hydroelectric U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroelectricity)___ systems.
Other sources of energy include the previously mentioned WCUP for building cooling and emergency backup electricity, as well as a number of solar installations across campus.

Buildings with ___E:solar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_power)___ installations include Mercer Court Alder Hall, Elm Hall, the Intramural Activities Building, Maple Hall, and the Life Sciences Building.

Although the majority of the university's electricity supply is carbon-free, the iniversity hopes to completely phase out natural gas from their heating systems and to be fossil fuel free by 2035 in regard to their direct emissions.

Research shows that there are many aspects that contribute to universities energy consumption, such as student activity, technology use, building types, systems efficiency, and more.  The university of Washington has addressed these aspects within their future energy goals.

From late 2023 into the end of 2024, the University of Washington created an actionable energy systems decarbonization plan with the help from an outside energy consultant team who assisted in assessing the campuses energy needs, existing systems, and energy goals.
